prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: i would be

outputs.L1:
I would be eight people,  
and then the difficulties would vanish.  

Only as one  
do I contain the complications,  
in a warm house  
roofed with the rib cage of an elephant.  

I pass my grey mornings  
re-running the reels,  
and the images are the same,  
though the emphasis shifts.  

The actors bow gently to me,  
and I envy them  
their repeated parts,  
their constant presence in that world.  

I would be eight people,  
each inhabiting the others’ dreams,  
walking through corridors  
of glass-framed pages,  
telling each other the final lines of letters,  
picking fruit in one dream  
and storing it in another.  

Only as one  
do I contain the complications,  
and the images are the same—  
their constant presence in that world.  

The actors bow gently to me  
and envy my grey mornings.  

I would be eight people  
with the rib cage of an elephant,  
picking fruit in a warm house  
above actors bowing,  
re-running the reels  
of my presence in this world.  

The difficulties vanish,  
and the images are the same:  
eight people,  
glass corridors,  
page lines repeated,  
inhabiting grey mornings  
roofed with my complications.  

Only as one,  
walking gently,  
storing my dream.
outputs.L2:
I would split into eight selves, and only when I am singular do the troubles disappear.  
Alone, I hold every complexity inside a heated dwelling, its ceiling made from an elephant’s ribs.  
I spend my ash-colored mornings playing the films again; the pictures do not change, though the stress falls elsewhere.  
The performers incline themselves softly before me, and I long for what they have: roles endlessly repeated, an unbroken existence inside that realm.

I would become eight people, each one living within the dreams of the rest,  
moving along passages of glass and bordered sheets,  
reciting to one another the closing sentences of letters,  
gathering fruit in one sleep and keeping it safe in another.  
Only as a single being do I carry the entanglements,  
and the scenes remain unchanged: their steady belonging to that world.  
The actors bend toward me with quiet grace and covet my dim mornings.

I would be eight persons under the elephant-rib roof,  
collecting fruit inside a warm house above performers who bow,  
spooling again the films of my being here.  
The hardships fade; the pictures stay identical:  
eight figures, transparent halls, repeated margins of pages,  
living inside pale mornings sheltered by my own complications.  
Only as one do I move softly, storing away my dream.
outputs.L3:
The speaker imagines becoming eight people as a way of making life’s difficulties disappear. This fantasy suggests a desire to divide the burden of existence among several selves, so that no single version of the speaker would have to carry everything alone. By multiplying the self, the speaker imagines escaping the pressure, confusion, and emotional weight that come with being only one person.

At the same time, the speaker feels that remaining a single individual forces them to contain many complications. One person must hold conflicting thoughts, memories, desires, and anxieties all at once. The poem presents identity as something crowded and difficult, not simple or unified. The speaker’s wish to become many people reveals how overwhelming it can feel to live with so many inner contradictions inside one body and one mind.

Throughout the poem, the speaker repeatedly returns to the same memories, images, or scenes. However, these repetitions are not exact copies. Each time an image reappears, its meaning changes slightly, or a different detail becomes important. This creates the sense that memory is unstable and layered. The speaker is not merely remembering the past, but continually reinterpreting it, searching for new meaning in familiar fragments.

The actors in the speaker’s imagined world seem constant and vividly present. They appear to possess a kind of stability that the speaker lacks, which inspires both envy and reflection. The speaker observes them as figures who remain whole and visible, while the speaker’s own sense of self feels divided and uncertain. Their presence becomes a mirror through which the speaker considers their own identity and inner life.

Overall, the poem blends dreams, repetition, and fragmented spaces to explore questions of identity, memory, and inner complexity. Its dreamlike structure reflects the speaker’s shifting mental state, while its repeated images show how memory can circle back on itself without ever becoming fully settled. Through this fragmented and imaginative world, the poem suggests that the self is not fixed or simple, but made up of many overlapping feelings, roles, and remembered moments.
outputs.L4:
The text explores fragmented identity, memory, and longing through surreal, dreamlike imagery and repeated phrases that shift in emphasis. Its language creates the sense of a mind circling around an unresolved feeling, returning again and again to the same images in the hope that repetition might clarify them. Instead, each return slightly alters the meaning, making the speaker’s experience feel unstable, layered, and difficult to grasp.

Throughout the piece, identity appears not as something whole or fixed, but as something divided. The speaker seems to imagine the self as multiple, as if there might be relief in being more than one person or in existing in several forms at once. This multiplicity suggests a desire to escape the limits of a single life, a single body, or a single emotional burden. If the self could be split, multiplied, or dispersed, perhaps pain would become less concentrated. Perhaps memory would be easier to carry if it were shared among many versions of the speaker.

Yet the text does not fully allow that escape. Even as it imagines multiplicity, the speaker remains trapped in singular experience. The burden cannot truly be divided; it continues to belong to one consciousness. This tension gives the work much of its emotional force. The dreamlike images open the possibility of transformation, but the repeated phrases pull the speaker back into the same place. The result is a feeling of suspension: the speaker longs to move beyond the self, but remains enclosed within it.

Memory also plays a central role. The text suggests that memory is not linear or reliable, but recursive and haunting. Images return not because they have been resolved, but because they have not. Repetition becomes the structure of remembering: a phrase or image appears again, carrying traces of its earlier use while gathering new associations. In this way, the text mimics the experience of being unable to let go of something. Memory becomes both a refuge and a prison, preserving what matters while also preventing release.

The repeated language is especially important because it creates both stability and confinement. On one hand, repetition gives the text rhythm and coherence. It offers something recognizable in a world of shifting, surreal imagery. On the other hand, the same repetition suggests entrapment. The speaker seems caught inside a pattern of thought or feeling, unable to move forward. What might first appear comforting gradually becomes restrictive, as though the repeated phrases are walls rather than anchors.

Longing moves beneath all of this. The speaker longs for release, for transformation, perhaps for connection with another person or another version of the self. But the text does not present longing as something easily fulfilled. Instead, longing becomes another form of repetition: a reaching that never quite arrives. The dreamlike quality of the imagery intensifies this sense of distance, making desire feel vivid but unreachable.

Ultimately, the text presents repetition as a powerful image of the speaker’s condition. To repeat is to preserve, to insist, and to remember; but it is also to remain bound to what cannot be changed. The possibility of multiplicity offers a brief fantasy of relief, as if difficulty might dissolve if the self could become many. Yet the speaker remains singularly burdened, caught between the desire to fragment and the reality of being one. In this tension, the text becomes a meditation on how memory and identity can both sustain and imprison the self.
outputs.L5:
**I Would Be**

If I could choose what I would be, I would be someone who brings calm into difficult moments. I would be the kind of person who listens before speaking, understands before judging, and helps without expecting anything in return.

I would be brave enough to follow my dreams, even when the path is uncertain. I would be patient with myself when I make mistakes, because every mistake can teach a lesson. I would be grateful for small things: a kind word, a quiet morning, a chance to begin again.

I would be a friend people can trust, a voice of encouragement when someone feels lost, and a light in places that feel dark. I would be strong, not because life is always easy, but because I would keep going even when it is hard.

Most of all, I would be myself—honest, hopeful, and always growing.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in lowercase about wanting to be eight people at once, using dream logic, repeated phrases, actors, old film reels, glass corridors, letters, fruit, and a house roofed with an elephant’s rib cage.
counterfactuals.output:
i want to be eight people at once, eight doors in the same glass corridor, eight actors forgetting the same line under different moons. i want to enter myself wearing a borrowed face and leave myself carrying fruit in my sleeves: pears like little green lungs, oranges humming with telegrams, plums dark as sealed letters from the dead.

in the old film reels, i am always walking away. in the old film reels, i turn back and become someone else. one of me is crying in a kitchen where the knives are asleep. one of me is laughing on a train that has no tracks. one of me is a famous actor made entirely of rain, bowing to an audience of chairs. one of me is a letter that never learned to be opened. one of me is the hand that opens it. one of me is the fruit rotting sweetly in the bowl. one of me is the bowl. one of me is counting and discovers there are nine, then seven, then eight again.

i want to be eight people at once. i want to be eight people at once. i want to stand in the glass corridor and watch my reflections disagree about the weather. behind every pane, another childhood is developing in a tray of chemicals. the reel clicks, the reel burns, the actors mouth words no one has invented yet. a woman with a fox’s voice hands me a letter addressed to “the one who stayed,” but all eight of us have left, dragging our shadows like black coats through the orchard.

somewhere there is a house roofed with an elephant’s rib cage. i live there, or i am dreamed there, or i am the house thinking of a body large enough to shelter me. rain plays the ribs like a xylophone. the attic smells of dust, bananas, and applause. in one room, an actor removes his face and finds another actor waiting underneath. in another, a child eats a peach and remembers being elderly. in another, eight beds sleep in one bed.

at night the letters crawl out of their envelopes and graze in the yard. dear impossible, they say. dear multiplied hunger. dear glass corridor, dear fruit with its small suns, dear old film reels coughing silver smoke into the ceiling. i answer them with all my mouths. i answer them in lowercase. i answer them by becoming the stamp, the window, the elephant, the roof, the rain, the actor, the audience, the door.

i want to be eight people at once, so no grief can find the correct address. i want to be eight people at once, so joy has to knock eight times before entering. i want to be eight people at once, and still, in the final reel, when the house kneels beneath its ivory bones and the glass corridor fills with fruit, all eight of me turn toward the camera, holding the same unopened letter, and whisper: i was always only one dream trying on many sleepers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical, surreal poem about multiplicity and memory, repeating motifs like grey mornings, bowing actors, dreams within dreams, glass-framed pages, and “only as one i contain the complications.”
counterfactuals.output:
In the grey mornings, I wake with many faces,  
each one rinsed in rain, each one whispering  
a different name into the basin.

Outside, the street unfolds itself  
like a glass-framed page—  
ink trembling behind the transparent weather,  
footsteps trapped in the margins,  
a bird crossing out the sky.

There are bowing actors in the hallway,  
their velvet sleeves full of dust and constellations.  
They bend, rise, bend again,  
as if applause were a tide  
and the world a theatre dreaming itself open.

I remember what I have never lived:  
a room inside a room inside a room,  
dreams within dreams,  
each door painted with the same grey morning,  
each window looking inward  
to another window.

Someone turns the glass-framed pages.  
Someone reads me aloud.  
Someone forgets the ending  
and so I begin again.

My childhood is a chandelier of rain,  
my future a mask left on a chair.  
All my lost selves gather in the wings—  
the child with moonlit hands,  
the lover made of smoke,  
the witness carrying a lantern  
through the museum of sleep.

The bowing actors return.  
They wear my voice.  
They wear my grief.  
They bow to the empty seats  
where memory sits multiplying,  
one shadow becoming seven,  
seven becoming a field of doors.

And in the grey mornings, always,  
the kettle sings like a small oracle,  
the mirror fills with weather,  
the bed remembers the shape  
of every dream within dreams.

I press my palm to the glass-framed pages.  
Behind them, my lives flutter—  
moths, maps, unfinished letters,  
cities drowned in silver.

I say: only as one i contain the complications.  
I say it to the rain.  
I say it to the actors still bowing.  
I say it to the dream that wakes inside the dream,  
to the page that frames the glass,  
to the morning that greys and greys  
until even forgetting has a face.

And all my selves answer at once,  
a choir of broken mirrors,  
a single river braided from many waters,  
flowing backward through memory,  
forward through mist,  
carrying the theatre, the pages, the dreams,  
the endless bowing of what I was  
into what I am.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a recursive prose poem in the style of a dream journal, where the speaker envies actors for their repeated roles and imagines eight selves moving through shared dreams.
counterfactuals.output:
Last night I dreamed I was writing down last night’s dream, and in the dream the page had already been filled by someone with my handwriting. It said: Last night I dreamed I was writing down last night’s dream. I envied actors then, the way they can return to the same doorway, the same line, the same grief under different lights. How merciful, to be given a room and told: enter again; become the person you were; suffer in the practiced place.

In the first dream, one of me stood in a kitchen filling a glass with moonlight from the tap. In the second, one of me waited at a bus stop where every bus was a childhood. In the third, one of me slept inside a theater seat while the actors onstage performed my ordinary morning with terrible beauty. In the fourth, one of me opened a suitcase and found it packed with eight smaller suitcases, each humming softly. In the fifth, one of me walked through snow that remembered my footprints before I made them. In the sixth, one of me was an actor playing the role of “the one who envies actors.” In the seventh, one of me watched from the wings, mouthing every line. In the eighth, one of me wrote this down and called it waking.

We moved through each other’s dreams like guests through adjoining hotel rooms, borrowing coats, names, weather. The kitchen self handed the moonlit glass to the bus-stop self, who drank and began to speak in departures. The theater-seat self applauded in sleep. The suitcase self unpacked a smaller version of me, who unpacked a smaller version of the dream, who unpacked a smaller version of envy: a tiny stage, a tiny actor, a tiny wound repeating itself until it became music.

I kept thinking: actors know how to be haunted on schedule. They die at eight o’clock and rise for applause. They fall in love by cue light. They can lose a father, a kingdom, a letter, a mind, and tomorrow lose it again with greater precision. No wonder I envied them. My selves were always improvising, missing entrances, forgetting which dream contained the staircase and which contained the sea.

Then the eight of us met in a corridor that resembled the inside of an eyelid. Each door had my face on it, but older, younger, asleep, lit from below. We agreed to trade roles. The one from the snow would play the one from the kitchen. The one from the theater would play the one from the bus stop. The one writing would play the one watching. The one watching would play the one who had not yet been invented.

We rehearsed until the corridor filled with mirrors, and in every mirror another rehearsal began. I said, I am tired of being singular, and seven mouths echoed, singular, singular, singular, until the word became a bell. I said, I want a part I can return to. The actors in the walls leaned forward with their painted sorrow and whispered: You already have one.

So I entered again.

Last night I dreamed I was writing down last night’s dream, and in the dream the page had already been filled. It said there were eight of me, but I counted nine: the kitchen self, the bus-stop self, the theater self, the suitcase self, the snow self, the actor self, the wing-watching self, the writing self, and the one reading over my shoulder, envying us all for being able to repeat.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
